statement: Let $\mathcal C$ be a proper [model category](c:model-category) and $Q$ an endofunctor with a natural map $\eta\colon \mathrm{id}\to Q$ that keeps weak equivalences, makes $\eta_{QX}$ and $Q\eta_X$ weak equivalences, and keeps the [homotopy pullback](c:homotopy-pullback) squares of condition (A.6). Then $Q$-equivalences, $Q$-fibrations and the old cofibrations form a model structure on $\mathcal C$.

hypotheses.text: The functor $Q$ and the natural map $\eta\colon \mathrm{id}\to Q$ keep weak equivalences, and $\eta_{QX}$ and $Q\eta_X$ are weak equivalences.
The functor $Q$ keeps the [homotopy pullback](c:homotopy-pullback) squares of condition (A.6).

conclusion: The $Q$-equivalences ($Qf$ is a weak equivalence), the $Q$-fibrations (fibrations whose unit square is a homotopy pullback) and the cofibrations of $\mathcal C$ form a model structure.

proofs.name: Bousfield-Friedlander construction
proofs.slogan: Check the model category axioms for the new classes, using properness and the homotopy pullback condition.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem, as an outline of Bousfield and Friedlander (Theorem A.7), with Bousfield's later version in Theorem 9.3. The long verification of the lifting property is cited, not repeated.

roles.why: Properness lets homotopy pullbacks respect weak equivalences, which every later step needs.
The conditions on $Q$ and $\eta$ make $Q$-equivalences satisfy two-out-of-three and contain all weak equivalences.
The pullback condition makes the factorization map a $Q$-fibration and gives the lifting property.

steps.slogan: Define the $Q$-equivalences and $Q$-fibrations and check two-out-of-three and retracts.
steps.detail: A $Q$-equivalence is a map $f$ with $Qf$ a weak equivalence, so two-out-of-three and closure under retracts follow from functoriality of $Q$. A $Q$-fibration is a fibration whose unit square is a homotopy pullback, and this class is closed under retracts too.

steps.slogan: Identify the new trivial fibrations with the trivial fibrations of $\mathcal C$.
steps.detail: A $Q$-fibration $f$ with $Qf$ a weak equivalence is a homotopy pullback of the weak equivalence $Qf$, so $f$ is a weak equivalence by properness. A trivial fibration of $\mathcal C$ is a $Q$-fibration because $Q$ keeps weak equivalences. So cofibrations lift against them, and every map factors as a cofibration followed by a trivial fibration.

steps.slogan: Factor each map as a $Q$-trivial cofibration followed by a $Q$-fibration.
steps.detail: Bousfield and Friedlander build this factorization from a factorization in $\mathcal C$ and a homotopy pullback along the unit $\eta$. Properness and the pullback condition show that the second map is a $Q$-fibration and the first map is a cofibration and a $Q$-equivalence.

steps.slogan: Show that $Q$-trivial cofibrations lift against $Q$-fibrations.
steps.detail: The first maps of the factorizations in step 3 have the lifting property against every $Q$-fibration; the proof uses properness and the pullback condition. A $Q$-trivial cofibration is a retract of such a map by the retract argument, so it has the lifting property too.

steps.slogan: Collect the axioms into a model structure on $\mathcal C$.
steps.detail: Step 1 gives the weak equivalence axioms, steps 2 and 3 give the two factorizations, and steps 2 and 4 give the two lifting properties. Every weak equivalence of $\mathcal C$ is a $Q$-equivalence and the cofibrations agree, so the structure is the left [Bousfield localization](c:bousfield-localization) at the $Q$-equivalences.

concepts.c:model-category: The theorem produces a new model structure on the same category.
concepts.c:homotopy-pullback: Q-fibrations are defined by a homotopy pullback square of the unit.
concepts.c:bousfield-localization: The new structure localizes the old one at the Q-equivalences.

source.ref: A. K. Bousfield and E. M. Friedlander, Homotopy theory of Gamma-spaces, spectra, and bisimplicial sets, in Geometric Applications of Homotopy Theory II, Lecture Notes in Mathematics 658, Springer, 1978, pp. 80-130 (Theorem A.7); see also A. K. Bousfield, On the telescoping homotopy theory of spaces, Transactions of the AMS 353 (2001), 2391-2426 (Theorem 9.3).
source.note: The five steps follow the verification of the model axioms in Appendix A of Bousfield and Friedlander; the lifting argument of step 4 and the factorization of step 3 are cited in full there.

statement: Let a symmetric $(v,k,\lambda)$ [block design](c:block-design) exist with $k<v$ and $\lambda\ge 1$: $v$ points, $v$ blocks, each block has $k$ points, each pair of points lies in $\lambda$ blocks. If $v$ is even, then $k-\lambda$ is a square. If $v$ is odd, then $x^2-(k-\lambda)y^2-(-1)^{(v-1)/2}\lambda z^2=0$ has a nontrivial integer solution.

hypotheses.text: A symmetric $(v,k,\lambda)$ [block design](c:block-design) exists: $v$ points, $v$ blocks, block size $k$, and $\lambda$ blocks through each pair of points.

conclusion: For even $v$ the number $k-\lambda$ is a square; for odd $v$ the equation $x^2-(k-\lambda)y^2-(-1)^{(v-1)/2}\lambda z^2=0$ has a nontrivial integer solution.

proofs.name: Rational equivalence of quadratic forms
proofs.slogan: The incidence matrix makes a quadratic form equivalent to a sum of squares over the rationals, and Witt cancellation turns this into a splitting quaternion algebra.
proofs.scope: All $v$ and $k$ of a nontrivial symmetric design. The even case uses only the determinant; the odd case splits by $v \bmod 4$.

roles.why: The design gives an integer matrix $N$ with $NN^T=nI+\lambda J$, where $n=k-\lambda$.
It gives $n>0$ and $k\ne0$, so the determinant is nonzero and Lagrange's theorem applies to $n$.

steps.slogan: Write the incidence equation and compute its determinant.
steps.detail: Let $N$ be the $v\times v$ [incidence](c:block-design) matrix and $n=k-\lambda$. Then $NN^T=nI+\lambda J$ and $\lambda(v-1)=k(k-1)$, so $n+\lambda v=k^2$ and $\det(NN^T)=n^{v-1}k^2$. Also $n>0$ because $k<v$.

steps.slogan: For even $v$, show that $n$ is a square.
steps.detail: The integer $\det N$ satisfies $(\det N)^2=n^{v-1}k^2$ with $k\ne0$, so $n^{v-1}$ is a rational square. The exponent $v-1$ is odd, so $n=n^{v-1}/(n^{(v-2)/2})^2$ is a rational square, hence an integer square.

steps.slogan: For odd $v$, split the form $nI+\lambda J$ along the all-ones vector.
steps.detail: Since $\det N\ne0$, the map $x\mapsto N^Tx$ shows that $q(x)=n|x|^2+\lambda(e\cdot x)^2$ is a [quadratic form](c:quadratic-form) equivalent over $\mathbb Q$ to $I_v$, where $e=(1,\dots,1)$. On $e^\perp$ it equals $n|x|^2$, and $q(e)=vk^2$ by step 1. So $q\cong\langle v\rangle\perp r$ and $nI_v\cong\langle nv\rangle\perp r$ for one form $r$.

steps.slogan: Absorb the factor $n$ into four coordinates at a time.
steps.detail: By Lagrange's theorem $n=a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2$. Euler's identity gives an integer matrix $B$ with $B^TB=nI_4$, so $nI_4\cong I_4$ over $\mathbb Q$. Hence $nI_{4m}\cong I_{4m}$ for every $m$.

steps.slogan: Cancel the common form $r$ in the Witt group of $\mathbb Q$.
steps.detail: By Witt cancellation, step 3 gives $[r]=[I_v]-[\langle v\rangle]$ and $[nI_v]=[\langle nv\rangle]+[r]$. For $v\equiv1\pmod4$ step 4 gives $nI_v\cong I_{v-1}\perp\langle n\rangle$, so $\langle1,-n,-v,nv\rangle$ has class $0$. For $v\equiv3\pmod4$ use $nI_v\perp\langle n\rangle\cong I_{v+1}$; then $\langle1,-n,v,-nv\rangle$ has class $0$. So the [quaternion algebra](c:quaternion-algebra) $(n,v)$, respectively $(n,-v)$, splits over $\mathbb Q$.

steps.slogan: Combine the cases into the two stated conclusions.
steps.detail: For even $v$, step 2 is the claim. For odd $v$, $n\cdot1^2+\lambda v\cdot1^2=k^2$ splits $(n,\lambda v)$. Bimultiplicativity gives $(n,\lambda)=(n,\lambda v)(n,v)$ for $v\equiv1$ and $(n,-\lambda)=(n,\lambda v)(n,-v)$ for $v\equiv3\pmod 4$. Both are trivial, so $x^2-ny^2\mp\lambda z^2=0$ has a rational, hence an integer, nontrivial solution.

concepts.c:block-design: The design supplies the incidence matrix and the equation $NN^T=nI+\lambda J$.
concepts.c:quadratic-form: The proof compares two quadratic forms that are equivalent over the rationals.
concepts.c:quaternion-algebra: A split quaternion algebra is the same as a solvable conic.

source.note: The theorem is due to Bruck and Ryser (1949) and Chowla and Ryser (1950). This proof uses the incidence-matrix equation, four squares and Witt cancellation over the rationals.

statement: Let $1\le q<x$ and $\gcd(a,q)=1$. The number $\pi(x;q,a)$ of [primes](c:prime-number) $p\le x$ in the [arithmetic progression](c:arithmetic-progression) $a \bmod q$ satisfies $\pi(x;q,a)\le \dfrac{2x}{\varphi(q)\log(x/q)}$.

hypotheses.text: The modulus $q$ and the bound $x$ satisfy $1\le q<x$.

proofs.name: Large sieve of Montgomery and Vaughan
proofs.slogan: Turn the progression into a sieve problem and bound the survivors with the large sieve inequality.
proofs.scope: An outline of Theorem 2 of Montgomery and Vaughan, which treats intervals $(x,x+y]$ and gives the stated bound for $[1,x]$. The explicit estimates of that paper are cited, not repeated.

roles.why: The condition $q<x$ makes the interval of $m$ long and keeps $\log(x/q)$ positive.
Coprimality means that no prime divisor of $q$ divides any term $a+qm$.

steps.slogan: Write the primes of the progression as $a+qm$ with $m$ in a short interval.
steps.detail: Each prime $p\le x$ with $p\equiv a\pmod q$ equals $a+qm$ with $0\le m\le x/q$, an interval of length $N\approx x/q$. Counting the $m$ for which $a+qm$ is [prime](c:prime-number) is a sieve problem.

steps.slogan: Remove one residue class modulo each prime $\ell\nmid q$ up to $Q$.
steps.detail: For a prime $\ell\le Q$ with $\ell\nmid q$, exactly one class of $m$ modulo $\ell$ has $\ell\mid a+qm$. For $\ell\mid q$ no class is removed, since $\gcd(a,q)=1$. A prime $a+qm>Q$ survives, so $\pi(x;q,a)$ is at most the number $Z$ of survivors plus $Q$.

steps.slogan: Apply the large sieve inequality to the survivors.
steps.detail: The arithmetic large sieve inequality of Montgomery and Vaughan bounds $Z$ by a quantity of size $(N+Q^2)/L$, where $L=\sum_{r\le Q,\,(r,q)=1}\mu^2(r)/\varphi(r)$ for this sieve with one removed class per prime.

steps.slogan: Bound the sum $L$ from below by $\frac{\varphi(q)}{q}\log Q$.
steps.detail: Since $1/\varphi(r)=\sum_{\mathrm{rad}(n)=r}1/n$, $L\ge\sum_{n\le Q,(n,q)=1}1/n$. Splitting off the part of $n$ built from primes dividing $q$ shows that this sum is at least $\frac{\varphi(q)}{q}\sum_{n\le Q}1/n\ge\frac{\varphi(q)}{q}\log Q$.

steps.slogan: Choose $Q$ in terms of $x/q$ to obtain the constant $2$.
steps.detail: The choice of $Q$ balances $N$ against $Q^2$: $Q^2$ is of smaller order than $N$ while $\log Q$ stays close to $\frac12\log N$, which gives the factor $2$. Montgomery and Vaughan treat all ranges of $x/q$ with explicit estimates, which gives the bound for every $q<x$.

concepts.c:prime-number: The proof counts the primes that survive the sieve.
concepts.c:arithmetic-progression: The primes of the progression $a \bmod q$ become the integers $a+qm$ to be sieved.

source.ref: H. L. Montgomery and R. C. Vaughan, The large sieve, Mathematika 20 (1973), 119-134 (Theorem 2).
source.note: Montgomery and Vaughan derive the bound from their large sieve inequality; steps 3 and 5 rest on the inequality and the explicit estimates of that paper.

statement: In ZF set theory no [set](c:set) has exactly the [von Neumann ordinals](c:is-ordinal) as its elements. Equivalently, the class of all ordinals is a proper class, and by separation no set contains every ordinal.

hypotheses.text: Sets obey the axioms of ZF, in particular separation and foundation.

conclusion: No [set](c:set) $x$ satisfies $y\in x \iff y$ is an ordinal.

formal.difference: mathlib states that the class of ordinals is not an element of the class of all sets, which means that it is not a set. It defines an ordinal as a transitive set with transitive membership, which agrees with the well-order definition.

proofs.name: The set of ordinals would be an ordinal
proofs.slogan: A set of all ordinals would itself be an ordinal, so it would belong to itself.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. A set containing every ordinal gives a set with exactly the ordinals as elements by separation, so only the second form is proved.

roles.why: Separation reduces the statement to exact sets of ordinals, and foundation forbids a set that belongs to itself.

steps.slogan: Assume that a set $x$ has exactly the ordinals as elements.
steps.detail: Suppose $x$ is a [set](c:set) with $y\in x$ if and only if $y$ is a [von Neumann ordinal](c:is-ordinal), that is, a transitive set on which membership is transitive. The aim is to show that $x$ is itself an ordinal.

steps.slogan: Show that $x$ is a transitive set.
steps.detail: Let $z\in y\in x$. Then $y$ is an ordinal, and every element of an ordinal is an ordinal, so $z$ is an ordinal and $z\in x$. Hence every element of $x$ is a subset of $x$.

steps.slogan: Show that membership is transitive on the elements of $x$.
steps.detail: Let $u\in v$ and $v\in w$ with $w\in x$. The set $w$ is an ordinal, so its membership relation is transitive, and $u\in w$. Under foundation a transitive set with this property is an ordinal.

steps.slogan: Conclude that $x$ is an ordinal with $x\in x$, which foundation forbids.
steps.detail: By steps 2 and 3, $x$ is an ordinal. Since $x$ has all ordinals as elements, $x\in x$. This contradicts foundation, which says that no set is an element of itself. So no such set exists.

concepts.c:set: The theorem says that the ordinals do not form a set.
concepts.c:is-ordinal: The assumed set is shown to be an ordinal, which gives the contradiction.

source.note: mathlib shows that a set whose members are the ordinals is transitive (IsOrdinal.mem) with transitive membership (IsOrdinal.mem_trans), so it is an ordinal that belongs to itself, against ZFClass.cmem_irrefl.

statement: Let $n\ge2$ and let $u>0$ be [harmonic](c:harmonic-function) on the punctured unit ball $B\setminus\{0\}\subset\mathbb R^n$. Then $u=bE+h$ on $B\setminus\{0\}$, where $b\ge0$, $h$ is harmonic on $B$, and $E$ is the [fundamental solution](c:fundamental-solution): $E(x)=|x|^{2-n}$ for $n\ge3$ and $E(x)=\log(1/|x|)$ for $n=2$.

hypotheses.text: The function $u$ is [harmonic](c:harmonic-function) on the punctured ball $B\setminus\{0\}$ in $\mathbb R^n$ with $n\ge2$.

conclusion: There are a constant $b\ge0$ and a harmonic function $h$ on $B$ with $u=bE+h$ on $B\setminus\{0\}$.

proofs.name: Spherical means and harmonic expansion
proofs.slogan: Subtract a Poisson integral, show that the remainder is a multiple of the Green function plus a removable part, and remove the singularity.
proofs.scope: The unit ball and every $n\ge2$. The construction fixes a radius $r<1$, and the result passes from $B_r$ to $B$ in the last step.

roles.why: Positivity gives $w\ge0$ near $0$ and lets Harnack's inequality bound $w$ by its mean.
[Harmonicity](c:harmonic-function) makes the spherical means radial harmonic and allows the expansion in spherical harmonics.

steps.slogan: Subtract the Poisson integral of $u$ on a sphere $|x|=r<1$.
steps.detail: Let $v$ be the Poisson integral of $u$ on $|x|=r$: harmonic on $B_r$ and continuous on its closure. Put $w=u-v$ on $B_r\setminus\{0\}$; then $w=0$ on $|x|=r$.

steps.slogan: Show that $w\ge0$ by the minimum principle with a small multiple of $E$.
steps.detail: For $\varepsilon>0$ the function $w+\varepsilon E$ is harmonic. It tends to $+\infty$ at $0$ because $u>0$ and $v$ is bounded, and it is $\ge0$ on $|x|=r$ because $E>0$ there. The minimum principle on small annuli gives $w+\varepsilon E\ge0$; let $\varepsilon\to0$.

steps.slogan: Compute the spherical mean of $w$ as a multiple of $E-E(r)$.
steps.detail: The spherical mean $M(\rho)$ of $w$ on $|x|=\rho$ is radial and harmonic, so $M=\alpha+\beta E(\rho)$. Since $M(r)=0$, $M\ge0$ and $E(\rho)\to\infty$ as $\rho\to0$, we get $\alpha=-\beta E(r)$ and $\beta\ge0$. Put $G=E-E(r)$, so $M=\beta G$.

steps.slogan: Bound $w$ by its spherical mean with Harnack's inequality and subtract.
steps.detail: Harnack's inequality on the annulus $\rho/2<|x|<2\rho$ gives $w(x)\le C\,M(|x|)$ for $|x|<r/2$, with $C$ depending only on $n$. Then $g=w-\beta G$ is harmonic, has all spherical means $0$, and satisfies $|g|\le(C+1)\beta E$ near $0$.

steps.slogan: Expand $g$ in spherical harmonics and show that $g$ extends harmonically across $0$.
steps.detail: The coefficient of a degree-$k$ spherical harmonic is $a\rho^k+b\rho^{2-n-k}$ for $k\ge1$, and it is $0$ for $k=0$ because all means vanish. The bound $|g|\le CE$ forces $b=0$, since $\rho^{2-n-k}/E(\rho)\to\infty$. So $g$ is a convergent sum of harmonic polynomials and extends harmonically to $B_r$.

steps.slogan: Assemble $u=\beta E+h$ and extend $h$ to the whole ball.
steps.detail: On $B_r\setminus\{0\}$, $u=v+\beta G+g=\beta E+h$ with $h=v-\beta E(r)+g$ harmonic on $B_r$. The function $u-\beta E$ is harmonic on $B\setminus\{0\}$ and equals $h$ near $0$, so it extends to a harmonic function on $B$. Take $b=\beta$.

concepts.c:harmonic-function: Every function in the proof is harmonic, and their spherical means are radial.
concepts.c:fundamental-solution: The singular part of $u$ is a multiple of the fundamental solution $E$.

source.note: The classical proof of Bôcher's theorem, as in Axler, Bourdon and Ramey, Harmonic Function Theory (2nd ed., Springer, 2001), in the chapter on positive harmonic functions.

statement: In a set theory with power sets and separation, no [set](c:set) $V$ has every set as an element: there is no set of all sets.

hypotheses.text: Every set $A$ has a [power set](c:power-set) $\mathcal P(A)$ that is a set, and every subset of a set is a set.

conclusion: There is no [set](c:set) $V$ with $A\in V$ for every set $A$.

proofs.name: Power set against Cantor's theorem
proofs.slogan: A set of all sets would contain its own power set, which contradicts Cantor's theorem.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem. The set $V$ is nonempty because it contains $\emptyset$, so $\mathcal P(V)$ is nonempty and the surjection of step 3 exists.

roles.why: The [power set](c:power-set) $\mathcal P(V)$ exists, and its elements are sets, so they lie in $V$.

steps.slogan: Assume that a set $V$ has every set as an element.
steps.detail: Suppose $V$ is a [set](c:set) with $A\in V$ for every set $A$. In particular $\emptyset\in V$, so $V$ is nonempty.

steps.slogan: Show that the power set of $V$ is a subset of $V$.
steps.detail: Every element of $\mathcal P(V)$ is a subset of $V$, hence a set, hence an element of $V$. So $\mathcal P(V)\subseteq V$, and the inclusion is an [injection](c:injection) from $\mathcal P(V)$ into $V$.

steps.slogan: Turn the inclusion into a surjection from $V$ onto $\mathcal P(V)$.
steps.detail: Fix $S_0\in\mathcal P(V)$, for example $\emptyset$. Define $f(a)=a$ if $a\in\mathcal P(V)$ and $f(a)=S_0$ otherwise. Then $f\colon V\to\mathcal P(V)$ is a [surjection](c:surjection), because each $S\in\mathcal P(V)$ lies in $V$ and $f(S)=S$.

steps.slogan: Contradict Cantor's theorem, which forbids a surjection from $V$ onto $\mathcal P(V)$.
steps.detail: By Cantor's theorem no map $V\to\mathcal P(V)$ is onto: the set $\{a\in V: a\notin f(a)\}$ is not a value of $f$. This contradicts step 3, so no such $V$ exists.

concepts.c:set: The theorem says that the collection of all sets is not a set.
concepts.c:power-set: The power set of the universal set would lie inside the universal set.
concepts.c:injection: The inclusion of the power set into $V$ is an injection.
concepts.c:surjection: A surjection from $V$ onto its power set is what Cantor's theorem forbids.

source.note: The classical argument that a universal set would violate Cantor's theorem, which is the observation of Russell that led to Russell's paradox.

statement: Let $f$ map the open unit disk $\mathbb D$ conformally onto a bounded domain $\Omega$ whose boundary is a [Jordan curve](c:jordan-curve). Then $f$ extends to a [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism) of $\overline{\mathbb D}$ onto $\overline\Omega$, and it maps the circle $\partial\mathbb D$ onto $\partial\Omega$.

hypotheses.text: The map $f\colon\mathbb D\to\Omega$ is a conformal bijection: [holomorphic](c:holomorphic-function) and one-to-one onto $\Omega$.
The domain $\Omega$ is bounded and its boundary $\partial\Omega$ is a [Jordan curve](c:jordan-curve).

conclusion: $f$ extends continuously to $\overline{\mathbb D}$, and the extension is a homeomorphism onto $\overline\Omega$ that maps $\partial\mathbb D$ onto $\partial\Omega$.

proofs.name: Length-area argument
proofs.slogan: A length-area estimate shows that $f$ has small oscillation near the circle, so $f$ extends, and the extension is injective.
proofs.scope: The whole theorem; such an $f$ exists by the Riemann mapping theorem. The boundary values are first shown to exist and then shown to be injective.

roles.why: Conformality gives the area bound by $\int|f'|^2$, and $f^{-1}$ is continuous on $\Omega$.
A [Jordan curve](c:jordan-curve) is a circle up to homeomorphism, so close boundary points cut off a small arc.

steps.slogan: Find short crosscuts near each boundary point by the length-area estimate.
steps.detail: Fix $\zeta\in\partial\mathbb D$ and let $L(\rho)$ be the length of the image under $f$ of the arc $\{z\in\mathbb D:|z-\zeta|=\rho\}$. Cauchy-Schwarz and $\mathrm{area}(\Omega)<\infty$ give $\int_\delta^{\sqrt\delta}L(\rho)^2\,d\rho/\rho\le\pi\,\mathrm{area}(\Omega)$. So some $\rho_\delta\in(\delta,\sqrt\delta)$ has $L(\rho_\delta)^2\le 2\pi\,\mathrm{area}(\Omega)/\log(1/\delta)\to0$.

steps.slogan: Show that each short crosscut ends at two close points of $\partial\Omega$.
steps.detail: The image of the arc has finite length, so it has end points $p$ and $q$. They lie on $\partial\Omega$ because $f$ is a homeomorphism onto $\Omega$ and $|z|\to1$ at the ends of the arc. Also $|p-q|\le L(\rho_\delta)$.

steps.slogan: Use the Jordan curve to show that $f$ has small oscillation near $\zeta$.
steps.detail: Close points $p,q$ of the [Jordan curve](c:jordan-curve) $\partial\Omega$ cut off an arc of small diameter, and the image of the crosscut with this arc bounds a small region of $\Omega$ by the Jordan curve theorem. It is the image of $\mathbb D\cap\{|z-\zeta|<\rho_\delta\}$, because the other part contains $f(0)$, which is far from $\partial\Omega$. So $\mathrm{diam}\,f(\mathbb D\cap\{|z-\zeta|<\delta\})\to0$.

steps.slogan: Extend $f$ continuously to the closed disk and show that it maps the circle onto $\partial\Omega$.
steps.detail: Small oscillation near every $\zeta$ gives the Cauchy criterion for $f(z)$ as $z\to\zeta$, so $f$ extends continuously to $\overline{\mathbb D}$. The image of $\overline{\mathbb D}$ is compact and contains $\Omega$, so it is $\overline\Omega$. A boundary point cannot map into $\Omega$, since $f^{-1}$ is continuous there; hence $f(\partial\mathbb D)=\partial\Omega$.

steps.slogan: Show that the extension is one-to-one on the circle.
steps.detail: Suppose $f(\zeta_1)=f(\zeta_2)=p$ with $\zeta_1\ne\zeta_2$. The images of the two radii form a Jordan curve in $\Omega\cup\{p\}$, and it bounds a region of $\Omega$ that is the image of one sector. So $f$ maps the circle arc between $\zeta_1$ and $\zeta_2$ into $\{p\}$. A function holomorphic in $\mathbb D$, continuous on the arc and constant there is constant (Schwarz reflection), against injectivity.

steps.slogan: Combine continuity, injectivity and compactness into a homeomorphism.
steps.detail: The extension is one-to-one on $\mathbb D$, on $\partial\mathbb D$ (step 5), and between the two since $f(\mathbb D)=\Omega$ and $f(\partial\mathbb D)=\partial\Omega$ are disjoint. A continuous bijection from the compact space $\overline{\mathbb D}$ onto the Hausdorff space $\overline\Omega$ is a [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism).

concepts.c:jordan-curve: The boundary being a Jordan curve gives small arcs between close boundary points.
concepts.c:homeomorphism: The extension is a continuous bijection from a compact space, hence a homeomorphism.
concepts.c:holomorphic-function: Holomorphy of $f$ gives the area formula and the reflection argument.

source.note: Caratheodory's theorem (1913) in the length-area form found in Pommerenke, Boundary Behaviour of Conformal Maps (Springer, 1992).

statement: Let $X$ be a smooth complete connected curve over an algebraically closed field of characteristic $0$, and $G$ a connected [reductive group](c:reductive-group). Then [D-modules](c:d-module) on $\mathrm{Bun}_G(X)$, twisted by half the canonical class, are equivalent to [ind-coherent sheaves](c:ind-coherent-sheaf) with nilpotent singular support on the [stack of local systems](c:stack-of-local-systems) of the dual group $\check G$.

hypotheses.text: The curve $X$ is smooth, complete and connected, over an algebraically closed field $k$ of characteristic $0$.
The group $G$ is a connected [reductive group](c:reductive-group) over $k$, with dual group $\check G$.

conclusion: There is an equivalence of DG categories $\mathrm{D\text{-}mod}_{1/2}(\mathrm{Bun}_G)\simeq\mathrm{IndCoh}_{\mathrm{Nilp}}(\mathrm{LocSys}_{\check G})$.

proofs.name: Gaitsgory-Raskin proof in five papers
proofs.slogan: Construct the Langlands functor, prove its compatibility with parabolic induction, and show that it is an equivalence.
proofs.scope: An outline of the five-paper proof of the de Rham, unramified case in characteristic $0$. Each step rests on a paper of the series, which is cited and not repeated.

roles.why: The curve gives the stacks $\mathrm{Bun}_G$ and $\mathrm{LocSys}_{\check G}$, and characteristic $0$ allows D-modules.
Parabolic subgroups and their Levi quotients of the [reductive group](c:reductive-group) drive the induction on the Eisenstein and cuspidal parts.

steps.slogan: Construct the Langlands functor from the automorphic to the spectral category.
steps.detail: Paper I constructs a functor from $\mathrm{D\text{-}mod}_{1/2}(\mathrm{Bun}_G)$ to $\mathrm{IndCoh}_{\mathrm{Nilp}}(\mathrm{LocSys}_{\check G})$ using Whittaker coefficients and Poincare series. The later papers show that this functor is an equivalence.

steps.slogan: Relate the functor to Kac-Moody localization through the fundamental local equivalence.
steps.detail: Paper II connects the functor with Kac-Moody localization at the critical level. It uses the fundamental local equivalence (FLE) between the local categories to compute the functor on localized objects.

steps.slogan: Prove that the functor commutes with parabolic induction.
steps.detail: Paper III shows that the functor is compatible with Eisenstein series and constant term functors. So on the Eisenstein part the functor is controlled by the same functor for the Levi subgroups.

steps.slogan: Show that the functor is ambidextrous on the cuspidal part.
steps.detail: Paper IV proves that the functor restricted to the cuspidal category is ambidextrous, so its left and right adjoints agree there. It also deduces the conjecture for $GL_n$.

steps.slogan: Prove the multiplicity one theorem and conclude that the functor is an equivalence.
steps.detail: Paper V proves the multiplicity one theorem for Whittaker coefficients. With the results of papers I to IV this shows that the Langlands functor is an equivalence, which is the conjecture.

concepts.c:reductive-group: Levi subgroups of the reductive group drive the induction on the parabolic part.
concepts.c:d-module: The automorphic side is a category of D-modules on $\mathrm{Bun}_G$.
concepts.c:ind-coherent-sheaf: The spectral side is a category of ind-coherent sheaves with nilpotent singular support.
concepts.c:stack-of-local-systems: The spectral side lives on the stack of local systems of the dual group.

source.ref: D. Arinkin, D. Beraldo, J. Campbell, L. Chen, J. Faergeman, D. Gaitsgory, K. Lin, S. Raskin and N. Rozenblyum, Proof of the geometric Langlands conjecture I-V, arXiv:2405.03599, 2405.03648, 2409.07051, 2409.08670, 2409.09856 (2024).
source.note: The five steps follow the five papers: I construction of the functor, II Kac-Moody localization and the FLE, III compatibility with parabolic induction, IV ambidexterity, V the multiplicity one theorem.

statement: Let $G$ be a [finite group](c:finite-group) of linear maps of a complex vector space $V$ of dimension $n$. The invariant ring $\mathbb C[V]^G$ is a [polynomial ring](c:polynomial-ring) if and only if $G$ is generated by pseudoreflections, the elements that fix a hyperplane pointwise (a [reflection group](c:reflection-group)).

hypotheses.text: The group $G$ is a [finite group](c:finite-group) acting linearly on a complex vector space $V$ with $\dim V=n<\infty$.

conclusion: $\mathbb C[V]^G$ is a polynomial ring in $n$ homogeneous generators exactly when $G$ is generated by pseudoreflections.

proofs.name: Chevalley's argument and the Jacobian count
proofs.slogan: A reflection group has polynomial invariants by Chevalley's lemma, and the converse follows from a degree count and a Jacobian comparison.
proofs.scope: Both directions, as an outline of the published proofs. The technical lemmas of Chevalley and the Hilbert series computation are cited, not repeated.

roles.why: Finiteness gives the averaging operator and makes $\mathbb C[V]$ a finite module over the invariants.

steps.slogan: Average over $G$ and split off a graded complement of the ideal $SR_+$.
steps.detail: Let $S=\mathbb C[V]$ and $R=S^G$. The Reynolds operator is an $R$-linear projection of $S$ onto $R$, $R$ is finitely generated and $S$ is a finite $R$-module. By Maschke's theorem the ideal $I=SR_+$ has a $G$-stable graded complement $H$, and Nakayama's lemma gives $S=R\cdot H$.

steps.slogan: Use the reflections to show that relations among invariants come from $I$.
steps.detail: Chevalley's lemma: if $G$ is generated by reflections and $\sum r_jh_j=0$ with $r_j\in R$ and $r_1\notin R(r_2,\dots,r_k)$, then $h_1\in I$. The proof is an induction on degree, because $h-sh$ is divisible by the linear form of each reflection $s$.

steps.slogan: Show that minimal homogeneous generators of $R$ are algebraically independent.
steps.detail: A relation of minimal degree, differentiated and combined with Euler's identity and the lemma of step 2, contradicts the minimality of the generators. So $R$ is generated by algebraically independent invariants, and $n$ of them because $S$ is finite over $R$. This is the direction from reflection group to [polynomial ring](c:polynomial-ring).

steps.slogan: Assume $R$ is polynomial and compute its degrees from Hilbert series and Molien's formula.
steps.detail: Generators $f_i$ of degrees $d_i$ form a system of parameters of the [Cohen-Macaulay](c:cohen-macaulay-ring) ring $S$, so $S$ is free of rank $|G|$ over $R$. Comparing the Hilbert series with Molien's formula at $t=1$ gives $\prod d_i=|G|$ and $\sum(d_i-1)=N$, the number of reflections in $G$.

steps.slogan: Compare $R$ with the invariants of the subgroup $K$ generated by the reflections.
steps.detail: By step 3, $S^K=\mathbb C[g_1,\dots,g_n]$ is a polynomial ring containing $R=\mathbb C[f_1,\dots,f_n]$. The [Jacobian determinants](c:jacobian-determinant) of the $f_i$ and of the $g_j$ are nonzero multiples of the product of powers of the reflecting linear forms, because their degrees equal $N$. So $\det(\partial f_i/\partial g_j)$ is a nonzero constant.

steps.slogan: Deduce $R=S^K$ and $G=K$, and join the two directions.
steps.detail: The finite map of affine spaces given by $f$ in terms of $g$ has constant nonzero Jacobian, so it is finite and etale, hence an isomorphism of the affine space. Then $R=S^K$ and Galois theory gives $G=K$, a [reflection group](c:reflection-group). With step 3 this proves the equivalence.

concepts.c:finite-group: Finiteness gives averaging and the finite module structure of $S$ over $R$.
concepts.c:polynomial-ring: The invariant ring is shown to be, or assumed to be, a polynomial ring.
concepts.c:reflection-group: The group generated by reflections is the group that gives polynomial invariants.
concepts.c:cohen-macaulay-ring: Cohen-Macaulayness of $S$ makes it free over a polynomial subring of parameters.
concepts.c:jacobian-determinant: The Jacobian determinant detects reflecting hyperplanes through its degree.

source.ref: C. Chevalley, Invariants of finite groups generated by reflections, American Journal of Mathematics 77 (1955), 778-782; G. C. Shephard and J. A. Todd, Finite unitary reflection groups, Canadian Journal of Mathematics 6 (1954), 274-304.
source.note: Steps 1 to 3 follow Chevalley's uniform proof that a reflection group has polynomial invariants. Steps 4 to 6 give the converse by the degree count and Jacobian comparison of the standard treatments of the theorem of Shephard and Todd.

statement: Let $L\subseteq\Sigma^*$ be a [context-free language](c:context-free-language). Then there are a finite alphabet $\Delta$, a [Dyck language](c:dyck-language) $D\subseteq\Delta^*$, a [regular language](c:regular-language) $R\subseteq\Delta^*$ and a monoid homomorphism $h\colon\Delta^*\to\Sigma^*$ with $L=h(D\cap R)$.

hypotheses.text: The language $L$ over the finite alphabet $\Sigma$ is [context-free](c:context-free-language).

conclusion: $L=h(D\cap R)$ for a [Dyck language](c:dyck-language) $D$, a [regular language](c:regular-language) $R$ and a homomorphism $h$.

proofs.name: Encoding pushdown runs
proofs.slogan: Encode the accepting runs of a pushdown automaton as bracket words whose stack part is Dyck and whose state part is regular.
proofs.scope: All context-free $L$, including $\varepsilon\in L$, which is the empty run. The automaton is normalized so that each move pushes one symbol, pops one symbol or keeps the stack, and it accepts by final state with empty stack.

roles.why: A context-free language is the language of a pushdown automaton, which supplies the runs to encode.

steps.slogan: Take a pushdown automaton for $L$ in a simple normal form.
steps.detail: A [context-free language](c:context-free-language) is accepted by a pushdown automaton. Replace each move by a short sequence of moves so that every move reads at most one input symbol and either pushes one symbol, pops one symbol or keeps the stack. A bottom marker makes the automaton accept by final state with empty stack.

steps.slogan: Encode each move as a short word of brackets and define the homomorphism $h$.
steps.detail: Take brackets $[_X,]_X$ for each stack symbol $X$ and a pair $(_t,)_t$ for each move $t$; $D$ is the [Dyck language](c:dyck-language) on all these pairs. A push of $X$ is encoded as $[_X(_t)_t$, a pop of $X$ as $(_t)_t]_X$, and a move that keeps the stack as $(_t)_t$. Let $h$ send $(_t$ to the input symbol of $t$ (or $\varepsilon$) and every other bracket to $\varepsilon$.

steps.slogan: Let a regular language force consecutive moves to fit together.
steps.detail: $R$ is the set of concatenations $e(t_1)\cdots e(t_k)$ of encodings such that $t_1$ starts in the initial state, the target of $t_i$ is the source of $t_{i+1}$, and $t_k$ ends in a final state. A finite automaton checks this, so $R$ is a [regular language](c:regular-language). The empty word is in $R$ exactly when the initial state is final.

steps.slogan: Show that $h(D\cap R)\subseteq L$.
steps.detail: A word of $D\cap R$ is $e(t_1)\cdots e(t_k)$ with matching states. Since it is a Dyck word, the brackets $[_X$ and $]_X$ are well nested, so each pop removes the symbol on top and the stack ends empty. So $t_1\cdots t_k$ is an accepting run, and $h$ gives the input that it reads, a word of $L$.

steps.slogan: Show that $L\subseteq h(D\cap R)$.
steps.detail: An accepting run $t_1\cdots t_k$ on input $w$ gives $e(t_1)\cdots e(t_k)\in R$ by the state conditions. The run pops only what it pushed and ends with empty stack, so the brackets are well nested and the word is in $D$. Applying $h$ gives $w$.

steps.slogan: Combine the two inclusions into $L=h(D\cap R)$.
steps.detail: Steps 4 and 5 give both inclusions, and $\Delta$, $D$, $R$ and $h$ come from steps 2 and 3. For $\varepsilon\in L$ the empty run shows $\varepsilon\in D\cap R$.

concepts.c:context-free-language: The language is the language of a pushdown automaton whose runs are encoded.
concepts.c:dyck-language: Well-nested brackets of the encoding express the stack discipline of the automaton.
concepts.c:regular-language: A regular language checks that the states of consecutive moves match.

source.note: The pushdown automaton proof of the theorem of Chomsky and Schutzenberger, The algebraic theory of context-free languages (1963), as given in textbooks on formal languages.
